summary: Defines a method for negotiating data compression over PPP links. It is on the standards track as a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: CCP lets the two ends of a PPP link agree whether to compress data and which method to use. It also defines reset messages so a decompression problem can be handled in one direction without stopping traffic in the other.

subtitle: How PPP peers negotiate compression and recover when compressed data cannot be decoded.

tldr.problem: Two ends of a Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) link need a shared way to negotiate compression and respond to a decompression failure.
tldr.mechanism: The Compression Control Protocol (CCP) reuses PPP's Link Control Protocol exchange with its own options. Reset-Request and Reset-Ack packets let the peers reset compression state in one direction.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1962 defines how PPP negotiates compression but does not require one particular algorithm. It is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 2153.

today: RFC 1962 is a Proposed Standard published in June 1996. It has been updated by RFC 2153.

sections.title: Compression Is Negotiated per Direction
sections.content:
PPP first uses its Link Control Protocol (LCP) to configure and test a link. Once the link is established, the peers may negotiate optional features such as data compression.

Many compression methods can be negotiated. Typically one method is used in each direction, but the two directions may use different methods or only one direction may be compressed. The choice can depend on speed, cost, memory or other considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: Before compressing traffic, the two PPP peers agree on a method. They can choose different methods for each direction, or compress only one direction.

sections.title: CCP Reuses the LCP Negotiation
sections.content:
The Compression Control Protocol (CCP) configures, enables and disables compression algorithms at both ends of a point-to-point link. It also signals compression or decompression failures.

CCP uses the packet exchange mechanism of LCP, but has its own configuration options and protocol field values. CCP packets use PPP Protocol field 80FD; individual-link compression across a multi-link connection uses 80FB. CCP adds Code 14, Reset-Request, and Code 15, Reset-Ack, to the familiar configuration and termination codes.

CCP packets may be exchanged only after PPP reaches the Network-Layer Protocol phase. Earlier CCP packets should be discarded. Implementations should allow authentication and link-quality procedures to finish before timing out while waiting for a response.
sections.plainLanguage: CCP follows the same negotiation pattern as LCP but has its own compression choices. It adds two reset messages for recovering from a decompression problem.

sections.title: Sending Compressed Datagrams
sections.content:
Compressed datagrams may be sent only after PPP reaches the Network-Layer Protocol phase and CCP reaches the Opened state. They use PPP Protocol field 00FD; when each link in a multi-link connection is treated separately, the field is 00FB.

Only one primary compression algorithm is active in each direction at a time, and it is negotiated before the first compressed frame. The protocol field says that a datagram is compressed, but does not identify the algorithm.

A compressed packet cannot exceed the maximum PPP Information field length. If compression makes data larger, it may be sent in standard uncompressed form or split into multiple datagrams if the algorithm supports that. Each algorithm must provide a way to check reliable operation or require a reliable transport.
sections.plainLanguage: Once the peers agree on a compression method, a special PPP field marks compressed traffic. That marker does not name the method because the peers have already negotiated it.

sections.title: Resetting After a Decompression Failure
sections.content:
Reset-Request and Reset-Ack handle a decompression failure in one direction without affecting traffic in the other. An implementation that detects a failure should send Code 14, Reset-Request. Until it receives a valid matching acknowledgment, it discards compressed packets and retransmits the request with the same Identifier.

On receiving Reset-Request, the transmitting compressor resets to its initial state, which may include clearing a dictionary or resetting hash codes. It must return Code 15, Reset-Ack, with the request's Identifier. When the acknowledgment arrives, the receiving decompressor resets too; it must reset for each acknowledgment matching the expected Identifier.

The Identifier must change when the request data changes or when a valid reply to the previous request arrives. It may remain unchanged for retransmissions.
sections.plainLanguage: If the receiver can no longer decompress data, it requests a reset. The sender resets its compressor and acknowledges, then the receiver resets its decompressor.

sections.title: Choosing a Compression Option
sections.content:
CCP options describe algorithms that the receiver can use to decompress data from the sender. A peer may offer several options, and the peers negotiate one for that direction. If they cannot agree, the link continues without compression.

An unknown option must be rejected. If a recognized option has unacceptable values, the peer responds with a Configure-Nak containing acceptable values. Option type 0 identifies a vendor-specific algorithm using an IEEE Organization Unique Identifier, subtype and vendor-defined values. Option types 1 through 254 identify other compression types; the RFC lists examples and notes that no particular technique had become an Internet Standard.

Before accepting a vendor option, an implementation must confirm that it can decompress that algorithm and understands its vendor-specific values. The RFC does not select a required compression algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side offers methods it can decode, and the peers settle on one. If there is no method they both accept, they send data without compression.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that security issues are not discussed in this memo. It does not define a security mechanism or offer security guidance for the compression negotiation described here.
